utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, good afternoon. Judge Nosworthy has still not fully recovered, and although she was able to sit in morning, sitting in the two cases has, obviously, taken its toll. So we have decided again to sit, in terms of Rule 15 bis, in her absence. Could we now have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We will continue with your evidence now. Please remember that the solemn declaration to tell the truth which you made at the beginning of your evidence continues to apply to your evidence today. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, K72. Last night, when we finished, we were talking about you having been required to do some work for the MUP. Can you tell us how you were paid for the work you did for the MUP. How often did you get paid? In what form did you get paid?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know it was very little. I'm not sure. Maybe around 10 German marks at the time for 15 days, maybe a little longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, when the police asked you to come do this work, how did you get to and from the places where you did the work for them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I came with my machine and that's the way I went back.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And were you transported from your house to where the machine was kept?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A car came to pick me up and drove me back home.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was that a police car?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What kind of car was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes it was a police car, sometimes an unmarked police car, because they had cars like that, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And who came in those cars to pick you up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know these people, but they were members of the MUP. They wore camouflage uniforms. I don't know who they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What colour was the camouflage uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Blue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now I want to go to paragraph 13 of your statement, K72. You describe there how sometime around April a MUP officer came to your home to pick you up to go do some delicate work, and you mentioned you were taken to the Bistrazin bridge area. How did you get to the bridge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether he was an officer. He did wear a uniform, a blue camouflage uniform, no signs of rank. So I don't know whether he was an officer. He took me to the place where the machine was parked, and then I followed the car to the point of destination.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we bring up Exhibit P615, please, at page 22.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness, I'd like to show you a map, and it will come up on the screen in front of you shortly. I would ask if you can see on the map where the Bistrazin bridge is located.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if we can zoom in on the area just to the east of Gjakova. If we could centre a little bit to the left of where the magnifying glass is now, and down. That's good. One more, perhaps one more, and maybe even one more, if possible. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness, can you see on that map where the Bistrazin bridge is? I don't know how big your screen is.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This thick blue line, I believe, is the Drin River. And there is another little river - it must be a thin blue line - the Erenik River, and that's where the bridge must be. The thin blue line, I simply can't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, the thin blue line you're talking about is the river that runs from Djakovica toward the bigger river shown on the map, the Drina, and connects with it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the bridge you're talking about is on what road?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Djakovica-Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I would trust that the Court can see where there is a location that fits that description of a thin blue line, being the river from Gjakova and the road. There is a location also by that name of Bistrazin on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How many -- you indicated in your statement that there were police officers there when you arrived. How many police officers were securing the area when you got there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number, but it could have been 10 or 15. It was night, so it was difficult to see whether all of them were in one spot. Or some were further away, maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And those policemen you saw out there, how were they dressed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Also, blue uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you know any of them either by sight or by name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not a single one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Had you ever -- well, let me strike that. You mentioned in your statement that this site, this grave-site, was pretty big. Can you give us a rough estimate of how big an area you're talking about, how many metres by how many metres.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps 4 by 7 or 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you describe how you started digging and realised you were digging up bodies. How many -- approximately how many bodies did you dig up at that site?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one policeman there told me when I asked him, How much work is there to be done - because I was already sick; I was vomiting - and he replied, Well, not many; 100, 120.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When you dug up those bodies, can you tell us -- can you tell the Judges in what conditions they were. Were their faces still recognisable or had they decayed beyond the point of being able to recognise faces?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were recognisable. You could see.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You say in your statement, in paragraph 13, that there were four to six Roma gypsies out at the site helping load the bodies. Did you recognise any of them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think I had recognised two of them because I had seen them twice on two locations. I wasn't sure, but they looked familiar. I believe they were from Djakovica or from one of the surrounding villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how were the Romas dressed? Were they wearing any kind of uniform or were they in civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In paragraph 13 you describe the vehicles that -- I'm sorry, paragraph 14, you describe the vehicles that were out at that scene. You describe the larger truck, and I think in your statement you referred to it as a refrigerated truck. Do you recall what colour it was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't recall the colour. It was not a very big truck; it was medium size, like the refrigerated lorry. And the refrigerated lorry was standard size.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did it have any markings on it that you recall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I noticed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what about the smaller truck? Do you remember anything about its colour or markings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't remember. I didn't really notice because it was night and you cannot see much by night and I was working. No, I did not notice anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what was its relative size compared to the freezer truck or the refrigerated truck?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately the same size, maybe slightly bigger, but I didn't pay much attention to that, to be quite truthful.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sometime after this event, did you see on television a story and pictures about a freezer truck containing bodies that was found in the Danube River?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in connection with that story, did they show a picture of the truck?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the picture was shown on television - I saw it - but one refrigerated lorry resembles another. I don't know if it's the same one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's my question, I guess. Was the one you saw out at the Bistrazin bridge where you were digging up bodies similar to the one you saw on TV?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm telling you, a refrigerated lorry is a refrigerated lorry. It was white. I don't remember any markings. It's possible that it's precisely that one; maybe it isn't. I couldn't really tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 15 of your statement, Witness, you talk about when there was a civilian convoy that was bombed. In your statement you say "the very next day," but during proofing you indicated to us you weren't sure about what day it was. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And that is one of the changes you wanted to make to your statement, was to indicate that you weren't sure about what day that bombing happened.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 16, you tell us about another digging job you did for the police, and this was at the Brekovac cemetery. Where is that cemetery located in relation to the town of Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if you have a map. It's next to the barracks. If you pass the barracks, you come up against Brekovac. If you go from the centre of town to the barracks, Brekovac is right there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can we try map -- Exhibit P615 again, the same page, and if we could blow up the are around or enlarge the area around the town of Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Are you able to see the area where the Brekovac cemetery was located?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If the usher could help you with the pen there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: There is a pen with which you can mark the map. Could you draw a circle around the area where the cemetery was located.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we take a screen shot of that and give it the next IC number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be IC86, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, you indicate in your statement that the police came to get you for this job and there were policemen at the site when you arrived there. Do you recall how many police were at the cemetery when you went to dig up bodies there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was also by night. There were quite a number of vehicles - I don't know exactly how many - and around 20 policemen that I saw there when I arrived. Vehicles were coming and going all the time. I don't know how many there were, but there were quite a lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in the course of digging up the bodies at the cemetery, you indicated you saw some grave-markers with names on them, on some of the graves that you dug up. Do you recall any of the names that you saw on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the names, but I believe, judging by the names, they were Muslims, almost all of them Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in connection with this dig, what kind of uniforms were the policemen wearing who picked you up and who were at the cemetery?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Also, blue uniforms, camouflage.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 17 of your statement, Witness, you mention one change that you wanted to make. In your statement it says that there was a big truck outside the cemetery and there was a smaller truck with a trailer. I think you indicated that you wanted to change your statement to reflect it was a tractor with a trailer inside the cemetery rather than a truck.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: With regard to the truck that was outside, how big was it compared to the refrigerator truck that had been used at the Bistrazin bridge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a trailer. Now, how big was it? Twice as big, I suppose, covered with a tarpaulin.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Twice as big as the refrigerated truck?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. You mentioned also that there were four to six Romas helping move the bodies from the cemetery to the truck that night. Did you recognise any of those Romas?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was probably the same team. There were two men that I had seen before, either there or in some other place, but there were those two that I had seen twice before in different places. I think they were from Djakovica or the surrounding area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So I understand, two of them were the same as two that you had seen out at the bridge when you dug up bodies there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you indicated, in terms of numbers of bodies, were there more or the same number as you had dug up at the bridge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there were more.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: These bodies, you indicated that mostly they were just individual graves, one body per grave, although there were a few in which there were two bodies. Were the bodies simply in the ground, in the dirt, or were they inside any kind of casket or coffin or other kind of container?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the ground, just in the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where is that reference, Mr. Hannis, to mostly individual graves and some with two?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If this is paragraph 17 --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I may have gotten ahead of myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- I have a question whether these were mass graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I perhaps skipped -- paragraph 16 there's a reference to: "I started to dig up individual graves."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I had that, but I didn't see there either the reference to some with more than one person.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I may be confusing that with the Guska but let me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Perhaps the nature of the graves in paragraph 17 could be clarified with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness, the bodies you dug up at Brekovac cemetery, can you tell us how were they, were they in one mass grave, were they in several individual graves? How many bodies per grave that you dug up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were individual graves, all of them. Now, whether I found only two bodies per grave in Guska or was it Brekovac, I don't know. But they were all individual graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. And you say in your statement you worked out there from -- well, from 9.00 in the evening until 9.00 or 10.00 the next morning, so 12 or 13 hours total?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I believe if there were more bodies than at the bridge there was something in excess of 100 to 120 bodies that you dug up during that 12- to 13-hour period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably, I believe there were more, and it took a longer time because this was a harder job because they were individual graves. I had to exhume them, then re-fill the pit, and there was a -- that took a longer time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you as a practical matter. In digging up an individual grave, approximately how long would that take you just to do one grave? How many times to you have to put your excavator in the ground to get the body out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two or three minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And these bodies, were you -- can you tell us anything about the state of decomposition that they were in, compared to the ones at the bridge, for example?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were recognisable.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe you indicated in your statement that you noticed what appeared to be bullet wounds on some of those bodies?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on some of them you would find these things too.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. After you finished the digging you told us in paragraph 18 of your statement how you went to what I think you referred to as the MUP gas station to refill. Was that a gas station that could only be used by the MUP at that time; is that why you called it a MUP gas station?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour, I think that this is leading as well, so my learned friend should put an open question to this witness in this regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't think this one is a leading question. I don't see anything wrong with that question. Carry on, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall the question or should I repeat it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I do. Well, I went to that petrol station very often, and I don't know that I didn't pay for the petrol and I had just assumed that it was a MUP's petrol station because I went there and I took petrol and I didn't pay for it. So it's just my assumption.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In paragraph 19 there was one addition to your statement that you made when we were proofing with you on the 24th. With regard to the number of bodies that you dug out of the forest area near Guska, do you remember approximately how many it was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I know that outside a building there were around ten bodies lined in three rows, three or four per row, whereas in the woods they were all scattered over the woods and there were many but I did not count them. I can't tell you the exact number.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was it more than ten?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How many police were out at that area when you went out there to go the digging?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would always see them in a group of 10 to 15, but as to whether there were more than that, I don't know. There probably were more of them securing that place.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how were these policemen dressed at Guska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Camouflage blue uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How did you know where to dig up the bodies in the forest?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: A policeman went ahead of me with a torch-lamp, and he would point me to the exact spot where the bodies were.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you mention in paragraph 20 that you were threatened by somebody from the MUP to keep your mouth shut. Where did that happen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Upon the completion of the job in Guska. I don't know this person. He approached me and he said that I shouldn't talk to anyone about the case, otherwise my head will be gone, as he literally put it. I told him that I had already told my wife and a lawyer. I used that as an excuse. I was afraid, and the truth of the matter was that I did indeed tell my wife but I never spoke to any lawyer about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You say this happened upon completion of the job in Guska. Where exactly, were you still at Guska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we were still there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And who was present when he made this threat to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one else, just the two of us. He approached the machine, and that's what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think there was one other correction that you wanted to make to your statement. In paragraph 23 the English version reads: "I was never engaged in collecting or digging bodies in the town of Djakovica. I do not know whether the mayor of Djakovica Momcilo Stanojevic was involved in these kind of," there's a word missing. I think you indicated to us that that word should be "operation."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Operation."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And in paragraph 26 you say you didn't take part in the removal of dead bodies of the Kosovo Albanians who were killed in Meja and Korenica in April 1999. I need to ask you how you know about that. First of all, were you ever at Meja or Korenica to dig up bodies?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was never there. I did go to Korenica before the war on one occasion to visit some friends, but I never went to either Meja or Korenica with any construction machinery.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But with regard to the bodies that you dug up at the Bistrazin bridge and in the Brekovac cemetery and at Guska, do you know where those people were killed, or where they were from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't know them, and I couldn't be able to establish that. I really didn't know where those people had come from.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have no other questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: The order will be: General Lukic, General Pavkovic, General Lazarevic, General Ojdanic, Mr. Sainovic, and Mr. Milutinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just give me one second to try to organise myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. K72, my name is Branko Lukic and I will have a few questions for you to clarify some things. Paragraph 10 of your statement. Before the bombing started, what was your combat disposition? Were you with the JNA or with the TO?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no combat disposition.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How did it come about? Weren't you supposed to be assigned one?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The army engaged me first at some point before the war. They asked me to dig roads for them and to make embankments for their equipment. I asked not to wear a uniform, and this remained so until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say that you were approached by a lieutenant-colonel from the VJ at Pastrik and asked that you work for them. Do you know what his name was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall. He was a stout person. The soldiers addressed him as lieutenant-colonel, although he wore no rank. And every morning I would have to report to the barracks and then things started moving.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There were two barracks in Djakovica. Do you know in which one the lieutenant-colonel worked?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I used to see him at Cabrat but not often. It is possible that he was in both. I don't know what his tasks were exactly, but I used to see him at Cabrat.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did he ever issue you with a summons or a call-up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was your work for the army entered in your military booklet?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 11 you say that the head of the State Security Service --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I seem to have to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you personally know Milan Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I only knew him by sight. I saw him on a few occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say that you did the same kind of job for the MUP as you did for the VJ. Do you mean camouflaging the vehicles? Did you make embankments and trenches for their equipment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say that the commander of the Territorial Defence was the city mayor of Djakovica, Momcilo Stanojevic, and that the TO asked you to dig trenches, bury cattle, and that you were ordered to do this by Slobodan Matanovic and Masan Rakovic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you say that they both wore blue overalls, or boiler suits, can you tell us were they monochrome blue?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were of a single colour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did they wear any belts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did they have any weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall. I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The colour of the boiler suits, did it resemble the monochrome police uniforms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It looked more like a worker's suit with blue trousers and blue jackets.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know any of those people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I used to know Masan Rakovic and this other one, what was his name, Matanovic, I used to work with them. I used to know them personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know what ethnicity were the people who were doing the work and wore the boiler suits, did they also comprise the Roma as well as the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the Serbs, they did wear such uniforms. I didn't see the Roma in those uniforms and I never saw any Albanians wearing such uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know that there were some civilian protection units in existence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know of the existence of the ones that I worked with, nothing apart from that. If that is the unit, that's the one I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you whether you knew that this type of uniform was not worn by TO units but rather but civilian protection units.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible. I worked with them and these are the people by their first and last name. As for the uniforms, I don't know. I don't know if there were any other units.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 13 you say that in April 1999 a MUP officer came to your house. You didn't know him, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You also say that your excavator was parked at the parking lot next to the MUP building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was it within the MUP compound or was it on the public parking place in front of the building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in front of the MUP building but behind the fence of the perimeter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that there was no one in the building at that time, since the MUP officers were moved out of the building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if they had moved out by that time, but this is where I picked up my vehicle and went to do the job.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The location you worked at was secured by the police, you say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You didn't know any of the policemen there, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 14, concerning the trucks that you loaded the bodies onto, they did not have any registration plates, did they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think they did have any. I didn't pay any attention, but as far as I can recall, I don't think they had registration plates.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You told us today that you saw no other markings on the trucks, is that correct, and you don't know where they went?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know the policemen who said to you that there were 100 to 120 bodies there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You personally could not estimate how many bodies there were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I could not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where were you when NATO bombed the Albanian column at the Bistrazin bridge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I was at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say that you were paid for the work you did in per diems. Who paid you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Someone from the MUP; I don't know who. He had a list and there was some drivers there, and I was the only excavator operator. He would pay us according to the list and according to the number of days he registered.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So you were not paid within the MUP building, but rather out in the field?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In both places, depending on where and how they would get the money.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are you telling me that in that period, in April and May 1999, some of the MUP offices were within the MUP building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the previous investigation I also stated that I couldn't remember dates and months. This was six or seven years ago. I know when the MUP building had been bombed because I saw it, but I don't know when they moved out. I only know that the third and the fourth floor were hit, and the building was demolished on those floors. I was working close by at the time, but I can't remember the month.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that the jobs you did were performed after the MUP building had been hit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I told you that the jobs were performed after the MUP building had been hit, would you accept that as a possibility?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether to accept it or not. I remember that the MUP building was hit and the person came - I think he was a Jew - and he took a picture of me on the excavator. And he toured the building that was hit that day. I was working for the army at the time because a pipe had been hit and it burst, and he simply took a picture of me. I think his name was Danijel Sifer, but I can't recall the date. It changes nothing for me. I know the things I told did happen, so it doesn't matter when.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. K72, it does change because you couldn't have been paid within the MUP building because at that moment it was shut down. There was no one there. No office was opened.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only wish I hadn't been paid there, but I was. I had been.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you sign a receipt?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I signed next to my name on the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say that you realised that the police were trying to cover up the crime. You are not familiar with the structure and the functioning of the MUP. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Therefore, you don't know what levels or what bodies within the MUP were involved in this possible cover-up. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You don't know who it was from the MUP and at what level they were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. I don't know who organised that and I don't think I ever stated anything of that nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 16 you say that two to three weeks before the end of the war you were visited by the police at 8.00 p.m. At that time it was already dark. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, maybe not fully. We waited until it was completely dark and then we set out.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Therefore, all of the jobs were carried out during the night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And that particular night you did not recognise any of the policemen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have established that only at those locations you recognised two gypsies which you had previously seen at the location in Bistrazin. May we conclude then that you did not recognise a single policeman who participated in these operations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: May we conclude that none of the policemen who participated in that was from Djakovica or its environs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of them may have been from the environs or from Djakovica, but I didn't know them. It was dark, they wore camouflage uniforms, and helmets and caps. It is difficult to recognise anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As for the MUP member mentioned in paragraph 20 who threatened you you told us that you didn't recognise him either?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said that he must have had a higher rank. Judging by his accent, could you have concluded from which part of the state he came?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Truth be said, no. He had no insignia, no rank on his uniform. He just approached me and I thought since he did that, he was probably an officer. And he just told me I should keep my mouth shut, otherwise I could lose my head, by those very words.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Among those killed you dug out, you didn't recognise anyone. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But for one man you say that he had a KLA symbol on his head?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And you say that all of them wore civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What sort of a KLA symbol did he have on his head?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was completely bald, shaven, and the only hair he had was the KLA symbol, the letters of the acronym.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I've asked you this indirectly, but just by way of conclusion I wanted to ask you this: You don't know who ordered and organised the digging out of the bodies?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 24 you mentioned that there was no place for Serbs in Kosovo and that you left Kosovo with your family. Why is there no place for Serbs in Kosovo anymore?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, in the part of Kosovo where I lived during peaceful times there were as little as 20 per cent of the Serbs, and not once those people moved out, of course there is no more room for Serbs there anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: K72, do you still live in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sepenuk -- oh, no, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't mind. I have only one question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] K72, in your statement you said that when the bombing started you were hired by the Army of Yugoslavia to camouflage their vehicles, and most of it was at Cabrat hill. You mentioned that that particular unit was an anti-tank brigade and that you were --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, anti-aircraft brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And that you were camouflaging Pragas. When you talk about Pragas are these anti-aircraft weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Someone else inserted that. I made embankments for various equipment. There were Pragas there as well as BOVs, the three-barrelled guns, but also some shelters and embankments for radar facilities. So most of them were Pragas and APCs or combat-armoured vehicles.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please repeat the question because he overlapped with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: It hasn't been entered into the transcript so I will repeat my question and the answer. At Cabrat hill there were on the anti-aircraft weapons. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: There were no tanks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no tanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, K72.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have no questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: K72, that brings your evidence to an end. Thank you very much for coming here to give that evidence. You are now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Kravetz, the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next witness is Liri Loshi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mr. Loshi is one of our Izbica witnesses and his evidence is primarily relevant to paragraphs 75(f), 77, and Schedule F of the indictment. He's going to be testifying pursuant to Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, can you clarify what we have here. We have the transcript from the Milosevic trial, and then we have certain statements.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes, we are -- were planning on tendering the transcripts of his prior testimony in the Milosevic case and then four of his previous statements, which were tendered into evidence in that case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, one of these statements is dated 2001, I think, and is a statement of about four pages. If you go to page 9423 of the transcript, at the foot of the page you'll see reference to a description in his statements of villages being surrounded. Now, that does not appear in any of the statements I have. And if you then go to page 9433, at line 11 you'll see Mr. Ryneveld referring to page 3 of a 31-page statement. Now, I certainly don't have that. Now, can I take it that there are statements that are referred to in this transcript that we are not to be provided with?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I believe the 31-page statement is the statement dated 23rd to 25th September, 2001.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I've got four pages of that in the bundle that was sent to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: There are two statements dated 25th September. One is dated only 25th September; the other one is dated 23rd to 25th September 2001. If we can pull up the exhibit if e-court, I think in e-court it's complete. And in e-court the exhibit number of this bundle of statements is 2436, and I believe the statement you're looking for starts at page 16 of this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So are there actually to be five statements given to us?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: No, there are four in total, plus a small very short addendum which is just one page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that makes five.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I only have four. I do not have the statement you're referring to. I don't know if my colleagues have it. We don't have it at all. Now, we normally rely on this material being submitted to us, and I certainly haven't read this 31-page statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: It was my understanding that the whole package has been submitted to the Chamber. This material had been submitted already at the time of our 92 bis motion, and I'm being told that on 24th October all these statements were provided. So unless there's some -- has been some confusion, it's my understanding that all the statements should be before Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There are attachments to the e-mail which have numbers of their own, starting with K022. Is there a particular number in that series that you can identify --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: It's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- for the statement over three days in September 2001?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes, the ERN range starts in K0226494.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: 6494. Now, that hasn't been included then.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: It starts in e-court as page 16 in e-court, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. We can --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If you would prefer, Your Honours, I mean -- I know it's early for a break, but if you want to review -- because I will be referring only to the statement which I now understand has not been provided to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we'll simply have it brought up on the screen as we reach the parts that you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So the usher will arrange that it's readily available.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I -- it's my understanding that hard copies will be provided shortly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that would also be helpful. Anyway, let's have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is one issue with one of the statements. I don't know if we want to discuss it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Hold on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The statement dated the 25th of September, 2001, the six-page statement, as far as I can tell deals with Padaliste, which is no longer part of these proceedings, so I think that one should be stricken from the record. So I think that the proper course of action would be to not admit that one and then not -- counsel's already indicated she's not going to ask questions about it, but as far as it's being admitted as a written document under Rule 92, I think that it's improper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes, this statement -- it is correct, one of the statements does refer to Padaliste. We have included it in the bundle of statements to be submitted because we have the witness here and we wanted to have him acknowledge that he gave that statement on this date. It may occur that in the future another witness will be referring to this witness in the context of Padaliste, not necessarily our scheduled incident but in the context of his activities in Padaliste. So we prefer to have this statement admitted at this stage just because the witness is already here. But I -- it is true that I will not be asking questions with regard to that statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it's not a good ground for admitting a statement that a witness happens to be here and can confirm that the statement was taken. It has to be relevant to the issues in the trial. And you're not making a submission to that effect, are you?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: My submission is that there may be another witness who will be called to testify at a later stage who might refer to this witness's testimony with regard to Padaliste, so in that context we seek to have this statement admitted. But I do understand Your Honour's point that this statement refers specifically to our scheduled incident which is no longer part of this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If that situation were to arise, you could then have this statement admitted in terms of Rule 92 bis if all that you sought was the admission of the actual statement itself so that someone -- to make sense of someone else's evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But it doesn't -- it's not appropriate to admit it in this context.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Well, I would agree to proceed with that course of action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That raises the other problem that the video which is shown in the Milosevic trial, is it the Izbica video rather than the Padaliste video?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So there's no issue over a video that creeps in via the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. We will exclude from P2436 the statement dated the 25th of September, 2001, and which is the shorter of the two statements that cover that date.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, let's have the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Loshi.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to tell the truth by reading aloud from the document which will now be placed before you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I would. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Do you propose to give your evidence in English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We've quite a bundle of material available to us from previous accounts you've given for the purposes of the work of the Tribunal. We have the transcript of your evidence in the Milosevic trial. We have the bulk of the statements which you've given. The reason for you being here today is so that counsel can explore with you further any particular areas that they wish more information about for a number of reasons. Because we have so much material already and because they wish to concentrate on particular areas, it's very important that you pay close attention to the questions and concentrate your answers on the particular questions that are asked of you so that we can get as much information as possible. We are not keen to go over again, except insofar as is necessary, the material you've already provided to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, the first person to ask you questions will be for the Prosecution and that will be Ms. Kravetz. Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. Could you please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Excuse me, I didn't quite understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I think you have to change maybe the channel, interpretation.

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: English, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes, number 4. Could you please state your full name for the record, Witness.

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: My name is Liri Loshi.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: When and where were you born, Mr. Loshi?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: I was born on August 20th, 1960, in the Padalishte, village of Padalishte, municipality of Skenderaj, or Srbica in Serbo-Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I understand from your evidence that you're a medical doctor by profession?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And is it correct that in March 1999 you were living and practising as a doctor in the area of Izbica in the municipality of Skenderaj?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: For how long had you been practising as a doctor prior to the war?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: For eight years.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mr. Loshi, did you provide statements to the Office of the Prosecution on 19th May 1999, and on 22nd May 1999, and then again on -- from 23rd to 25th September 2001?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Have you recently had the opportunity to review these statements?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And apart from making some minor corrections and providing some additional information, which has been disclosed to the Defence after your proofing session, are you satisfied that these statements accurately reflect the truth of the events that you describe in these statements to the best of your knowledge and recollection?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this point I seek to tender Exhibit P2436, with the exclusion of the first statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: -- that we discussed earlier.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mr. Loshi, did you also testify in the Milosevic case on 3rd September 2002?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And at the time, was the testimony that you gave there true and accurate to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: To best of my knowledge, it was truth and correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And if today you were asked the same questions that you were asked at the time of your testimony, would you provide the same answers?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: I will try.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender P2437 at this time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mr. Loshi, on page 4 of your statement dated 23rd to 25th September 2001 - this is page 19 in e-court of the English and page 17 in e-court of the B/C/S version - you describe how on 20th March, while you were in the village of Tushille, some women approached you and told you that when they were in the village of Izbica and they had been separated, the women and children had been separated from a group of men, and that the group of men had been taken away and that later the women had heard gun-fire.

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: This would be true except the date. You're asking me about the 20th of March, which is not the case. It should be by March 29th because the event of Izbica was by March 28th. And by March 20th you have another event, the previous event, which happened in Serbica.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes. I'm asking you about the event dated 28th March, that's correct. I think that's a mis --

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Okay. So would you be kind, then, to put to me a certain question you would be asking.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes, I was about to do that before you interrupted me, Mr. Loshi.

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: These women, when they approached you, did they explain to you who had separated the men and taken them away?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Again, please, you're --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I'm referring to the incident that was described to you when you were in Tushille on --

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Okay. So you're. Asking me about the event that happened in Izbica by 28th of March?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Okay. Now I know what you're referring to. And you wanted me to describe how they approached me and stuff like that?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes. What exactly did they tell you when they approached you on -- while you were in Tushille, these women from Izbica.

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Yeah. They came -- I was there on purpose of hiding myself from Serbian forces because everybody was escaping and trying to save their lives, so did I. And these women on the day of -- of 29th -- 28th came from -- from Izbica to Tushille in order to escape themselves as well and get refuge there, like other -- almost 20 to 25.000 people had gotten already there. And I met some of these women and they told me what they had experienced there. I was told by a woman - and I don't remember exactly her name - who told me that some, some -- I mean all of men who were in -- amongst the women and children have been separated and taken away by Serbian forces. And she said that even her father-in-law had been there. And these women, after the men had been separated and taken away, these women were chased in a different or opposite direction. So she said that right after that she could hear a gun-fire. That means she wouldn't see anything else except that she -- she heard gun-fire, and she assumed that all these men or most of them might have gotten killed by Serbian forces, including her -- her father-in-law.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: May I interrupt you there, Mr. Loshi. On the same page of your statement you indicate that on 30th March you decided to go to Izbica to find out for yourself what had occurred there. What were you able to discover about this incident that had been described to you the previous day, once you arrived to Izbica?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Once I arrived there, it was just like you said, 30th of March, and it was the evening, because the Serbian forces during the day were still there. So I was waiting -- I was looking at them from a distance, from the village of Kopiliq, and I was waiting for them to go away so I could get into Izbica and see with my eyes what had happened and what I was told the previous day from the women I met in Tushille. So by the evening sometime, the Serbian forces left Vojnik and Izbica, and I was able to see them with my own eyes. And then I moved there in the evening and I went to the massacre scene, because I met some guys there, some people, who led me to the massacre scene. And it was a little bit dark so I couldn't see well all that -- the horrible things that happened. But I saw dead bodies lying down and -- and been shot and with their faces disfigured and stuff like that, but I wasn't able to see quite well everything at that night.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And going back a little bit with what you were saying you said you were able to see Serbian forces from Kopilic. What exactly do you mean by "Serbian forces"? Are you referring to the army, to the police, to a different type of unit? Who you were able to see?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: I always myself used to call Serbian forces and even in the statement I gave to the Tribunal of The Hague, I never mentioned any other -- any other terminology except Serbian forces, because what I mean by Serbian forces is what it was in reality. They were all together. There were army forces, police forces, and paramilitary forces collaborating all the time together. So I myself at that day, if you are asking me for a particular day, I saw those green trucks and other vehicles going by, so this was what I saw from the Kopiliq was these army vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You said that when you arrived to Izbica you met some guys there and they led you to the massacre scene. Who were these people that led you to the massacre scene?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: I remember there was a leader of the village of Izbica who during these days he was hiding himself, and his name was Naim Rexhepi. I met him and he told me what had happened there. So we all together went together. And with me was -- was Shaban Dragaj, who was a commander-in-chief of the so-called brigade of the KLA. It was so-called brigade -- Brigade 112 of KLA, and he was a commander-in-chief. So we went together and we saw the scene.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You said that it was dark and that -- but that you could see the bodies.

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You indicated in proofing, and this -- I'm referring to the almost-to-last paragraph on page 4 of your statement of the same date that you wish to correct the fact that there it says that when you arrived you could not see the bodies from the massacre.

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: That's correct. That -- means I saw the bodies, I could see the bodies, but when it's dark nobody can see the bodies well. So that's what I was referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Did you return to these -- this location where you were able to find these bodies the next day --

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: -- in the daylight?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Yes, I did. In the early morning, next day, I went there and I -- I was able to see more closely what happened there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And what did you see at the -- at that location?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Once I entered the village, I went again to the same place I went the night before. And I saw these -- these men -- almost all of them old men except a few of them who might have been younger, a little bit younger. And I saw them lay -- lying down on the ground, dead bodies. There was a large group of all these -- these bodies, and there were two groups in the meadow just close to the mountain where -- so you have an edge there, and there is -- there is some bushes there. So just close to those bushes there was a large group of people massacred there, and this was the biggest number that I saw. And then I went into the bushes and I saw some smaller group of people, say two, three people, around. All of them were scattered around. And little bit further you go and you again find another -- another troop and stuff like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mr. Loshi, you indicate in your statement that you tried to find a camera to be able to film this, and you together with Sefedin Thaqi proceeded to film these bodies. Were you together with him throughout when he was filming these -- these bodies at the different locations?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Unfortunately not. I was -- I wished I was with him all the time, but, you know, when you are a doctor in those kinds of situations and you have -- you are the only physician there, and you have the people that have gone through massacres and people who had lost their loved ones and you have them waiting for your help. So I had to go all around and help people and sometimes go and watch Sefedin Thaqi how he was doing with his filming and stuff like that. So I wasn't all the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think the copies of the statements have just arrived and will be distributed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I would like to play a small video-clip at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mr. Loshi, that will appear on your screen before you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mr. Loshi, did you recognise the images that were just played before you?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Are these the groups of people that you found in Izbica --

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: -- that you were are describing earlier?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: We saw on the video bodies that appeared to be at two different locations.

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: The first group of bodies appear to be at an area with bushes. Are these bodies that you yourself observed?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Yes. These are the -- the bodies that I observed by 29th of March in the evening when I observed -- when I referred to what was dark, and next day, the morning. And the other group is -- is in different place, apart from this group. The first group would be to the west, what we call, from the place where they were taken from, and the second group would be to the east.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And referring now to the first group, approximately how many bodies, just very roughly, did you find there at that location?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Yeah, I never counted, myself, bodies. What -- I would say there might have been approximately 60, maybe 70 people. But I'm -- I cannot be specific about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And you were referring to finding elderly men. Were -- what was the age, approximately, of the bodies that you saw at these locations?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: The -- an average age that these people I saw and what -- because after that I was able to have a list of all these people that were massacred in -- in these two large groups. I would say between 60 and 70, even it might be higher, a higher age. It means they were very old.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Did you see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Kravetz, would you find a suitable point at which to interrupt.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: We can interrupt here, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is there a number for the video we've just seen, an exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I believe it's P232.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And that is an extract from a larger exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: That is an extract from a larger exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the larger exhibit is; do you know?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: That is the number for the larger --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: P232, and that is just part of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: That's just part of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Loshi, we have to interrupt now for 20 minutes. The usher will show you where you can wait, and we'll see you at five minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We'll adjourn until then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mr. Loshi, just a couple of questions regarding the images we just saw before moving on. From the bodies that you observed, did you see any of these bodies in any type of uniform?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And what type of injury did you observe, if any, on the bodies that you personally saw?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Yeah, I observed the injuries that were caused by -- by bullets in their -- in their faces, in their heads, in their bodies, mostly in their faces because they had clothes on. So I saw those bullet wounded -- wounds in their faces. And those wounds were pretty big, so most of their faces were pretty much destroyed and like -- very much destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Were you able to personally identify any of the bodies you saw at either of these locations?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Who did you identify among the victims?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: I must say that in the first group I knew lots of people. I couldn't tell them by their names -- I mean not all of them by the names, but I remember there was, for example, in the first group there was Metush Dogaj -- Metush Celaj [phoen]. There was Iljaz Bajraj and some other of his cousins with the last name Bajraj as well. In the other group what I mostly remember was three of my cousins which I used to live close to them in my village which is called Padalishte. And these were three people that belonged to three different generations from the same family, which was Selman -- Selman, 82 years old at that time, of execution; his son, Jashari, who was around 50 years old; and his -- and Jashari's son, Sami, who was around 25 years old. And then I saw in the -- in the same -- in this group where my cousins were were these people that just we saw with the [indiscernible] and sticks and stuff like that. So this is the -- the group with my cousins were.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. We saw in the images only bodies of male victims. Did you also find any female victims?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Not at those places where these people were shot -- I mean there-- where they were found. There were no females.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And in other --

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Not at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And in other locations around Izbica?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: There was a woman who I believe was killed in the place where all the victims were -- I mean all the -- these refugees were -- were at -- were trying to get a shelter or to get refuge. I believe she was -- she was burnt in a tractor, and then same woman was buried in this burial site where we buried all the others.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay, Mr. Loshi --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Kravetz, are these names on the schedule?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I believe some of them are, Your Honour. The --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I mean, that's very distinctive evidence about three generations in one family.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, these were my cousins --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- killed in this massacre, as I understand it. I don't see them on the list, unless I'm looking in the wrong place.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I do not see the names --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could you repeat the last names of your --

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Loshi, L-o-s-h-i, the same as my last name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: They are there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I think they are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, they are there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sami, Jashari, and Selmi. It was just incorrectly noted in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mr. Loshi, I would just like to play a second video clip.

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could you stop the clip.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mr. Loshi, did you recognise the images that were just played?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Sure I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could you explain to us what it was that we were just seeing there.

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: This was the place where initially the people who wanted to get refuge were gathered, and this is the very place where they were taken away from Serbian forces in many -- in two different directions. One group, like I said, in the east; and other one into the west. And from this place, all women and children were taken in a different direction again in the way to another village, which is called Turiqevc.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: What is the source of this information that you just gave us, because I know that you were not there on the 28th of March when this occurred.

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: I have -- I have gathered -- I have collected myself all the information, all the relevant information after -- after I went in Izbica because I wanted to make the case clear, I wanted to -- to have the event filmed. I wanted to have the list of names which we provided it, and I wanted to have some survivors' statements, which I provided the Tribunal with my tape. And also I wanted to know everything about what -- what happened there. So I talked to different people, and that's what I figured out. And I, myself, saw these -- as you see you now, I saw them with my own naked eyes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: We --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Kravetz, again, is this the same video?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: This is the same video, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the reference that the witness has just made to having "some survivors' statements, which I provided the Tribunal with my tape," are the statements on the video as well?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: They are on the video; they are towards the end of the video. The statement dated 23rd to 25th of September describes everything that is on this video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mr. Loshi, in that video-clip we just saw we saw several burned tractors and cars. Did the survivors with whom you spoke explain to you how this had come about, who had burned these cars and tractors?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: They -- they were describing the situation, what happened there, just like I told. All the people were -- were taken away and taken in three different directions. And then they burnt all cars and tractors that were there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: When you say "they," who do you mean?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: I mean -- by "they," I mean Serbian forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. I would like to play a fourth -- a third video-clip, a very short one.

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mr. Loshi, are the images we just saw also part of the video you filmed that day?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And could you describe to us what was taking place there in that part of the video.

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: What we saw here is a burial where we buried all the -- these bodies that were found in those places that I was just describing before, and also all other victims in Izbice that were found in some other different spots were brought here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Where exactly -- what location is this? Where exactly were the victims buried?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: This location is very close to the location where they were concentrated to find the refugees, where the tractors -- you just saw in a previous image. That means just a few steps into the -- into the left, or into the east, from that place where they were -- they were concentrated, where they were trying to hide themselves from shelling.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: We saw on the image a person in a uniform or part of a uniform. Where there members of the KLA present during this burial?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Yes.
