utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Were the persons buried that day only persons that died in that massacre or were other persons also buried with the victims of the massacre?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: All the -- first of all, all the victims that were found in those large groups were buried there, and except them there were few people that were found in some other locations very far to this place, which is still Izbica. Most of them -- some of them were just apart -- a few steps apart from these large groups, and I always assumed that these were the guys from the same groups again who might have tried to survive after they were shot and they were trying just to get into the bushes, and they couldn't make it any longer so they just fell down and -- but there were some other -- other few -- few people that were found little bit farther and they were buried there as well too. And there were two soldiers of KLA who died -- who were killed by Serbian forces again on the March of 27th, a day before this massacre happened. And this was in Izbica still but in a different location completely. I mean, it was pretty far away. Like, I believe it was a kilometre away from that place. Maybe less than a kilometre, 700 to 800 metres away from that place.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Can I stop you there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: One of the descriptions you gave was that there were a few "that were found in some other locations very far to this place, which is still Izbica." Now, what do you mean by "very far to this place"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I never -- I never meant to say "very far," and the reason I am taking my testimony today in English is that I don't want to happen like last time because I figured out myself that during the interpretation there have been so many mistakes that I don't want to go through that once again. Even English is my second language, I decided to take this testimony in English, so everybody could hear straight for word from my mouth what I'm talking about. These were not very far away. These troops, these bodies, were farther from these -- from the larger -- the large groups that we found, but they were still in Izbica. And Izbica itself, even if you say "very far away," you can say that because it's a small village. So that doesn't make sense. I might have even said that myself --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you did --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- but you've also just described "pretty far away" as 7 to 800 metres.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, these were two soldiers, KLA soldiers that were found, like, 7 to 800, maybe less, maybe more, away from this area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That clarifies the position for me. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You just spoke about two KLA soldiers being found there killed. Are you aware of whether there was any KLA presence in Izbica on 28th March from the information you were able to gather from others?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: I can tell by the names. I believe there might have been some soldiers of KLA around because they were trying to hide themselves. As it happened, all over Drenica in these situations when you have shelling from Serbian forces, very hard shelling, and, yeah, they might have been somewhere in the mountains, but I know that there was none of them in these groups where they were taken from women and children.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And how do you know this?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: I know from a statement I got from women, from statements I got from witnesses I have provided with a tape, and from all the people that were there. Nobody talked about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Are you aware of whether there were any clashes between members of the KLA and Serb forces on or around the 28th of March in the area of Izbica?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Not at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Loshi, moving on to another subject. You state in your -- in your evidence, in your written evidence, that a month later after filming the -- this -- these sites you left Izbica and Kosovo and headed to Albania to try to distribute the tape. Did you later return to Kosovo after the war?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I returned to Kosovo after NATO got in. I was there by 22nd of June and went to Izbica. And now I had my own camera. I provided in Tirana, the capital of Albania, where I was staying during that period of time. So I used it to tape -- to tape that burial site which was -- which was with no graves anymore. There were no bodies, no graves. Everything was flattened.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: What do you mean there were no graves?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: I mean --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Who -- where -- who had removed -- do you know who had removed the bodies?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: I was told, of course, that they were removed from Serbian forces during May sometime where still they had power in Kosovo, like where NATO hadn't gone in yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Who provided this information to you, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: I can't be specific in that because everybody talked about this. I mean, everybody that you met would tell you about this, so why would I pay attention who said this to me? And I didn't see this important at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And do you have any information to where these bodies were taken, as to where these bodies --

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: I just heard rumours. Like they were taken -- somebody said they were taken again in two directions. Somebody said they were taken in the direction of Klina, which is on the right side when you go to Turiqevc, and somebody else told me that later on they were found in Mitrovica somewhere. But this information wasn't clear to me, so I don't know much about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. Very well. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, these are all my questions for this witness. I would like to tender this witness -- the video that this witness has been referring to which is Exhibit P232. There are also a set of photographs which are still photos from the same video which are referred to in his statement dated 23rd to 25th September 2002 -- 2001, and these are Exhibits P230 and 231.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, these will be admitted. The other film that's just been referred to taken after the 22nd of June isn't an exhibit, I don't think?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I don't think that's an exhibit in this case.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I never brought the tape here because I was never asked for that. But if the Prosecution needs that, I would provide them with it, if they need it as an evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, first will be counsel for General Lukic, and then we'll follow the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Dr. Loshi. My name is Dan Ivetic, and I'm one of the attorneys representing Sreten Lukic relative to these proceedings. I have some questions for you here today with which I hope to clear up some matters from your various statements and your testimony here today. Therefore, it's very important for you to pay close attention to the questions that I ask so to ensure that your answers directly and concisely relate to the questions that I ask, because we do have some time constraints with respect to your testimony. Now, at the beginning of the statement dated the 23rd and 25th of September, 2001, you state that when you left Padaliste you spent some time in the village of Leocina, or Leqin in the Albanian. With whom did you live in this village after you had left Padaliste?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: I lived with -- in the family of Demush Dragaj, who was my close friend. I lived in this family -- with this family, in their house.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And is Demush Dragaj related to your other friend Shaban Dragaj?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: They are related to each other, but Shaban Dragaj was a KLA member and a KLA komandir, while Demush, who I stayed with, wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And are both Demush and Shaban also related to Mustafa Dragaj?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: They are distant cousins, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, during the time-period that you spent in Leocina, or Leqin, were there supporters of the KLA in the village at that time?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Initially they weren't. Like, I -- I can't remember where, but KLA was a very small group and they started to grow. And as it was growing, then they got everywhere, in Leqin, in Padalishte and Izbice and Vojnik and everywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Would it be correct to state that prior to March 24th in the year 1999, although they kept a low profile the UCK/KLA actually controlled Leqin, or Leocina, and the surrounding areas in the Srbica municipality?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. How many KLA personnel were located in Leocina during the time-period that you were there?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now during the time-period that you were in Leocina, am I correct that the local Serbs from that village had already left and that by that time the population was exclusively Albanian by 1999, the beginning of 1999?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: I am not quite sure, but I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I'd just like to discuss and clarify your various employment positions very briefly. Now, according to your statements, which we've read so we don't need you to repeat everything there, you were a reporter for an Albanian TV station from June 1998 onwards and also joined a medical team in the village of Turiqevc I think at approximately that same time.

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you go on to state that you helped the UCK/KLA by first treating soldiers and then, in fact, joined that organisation, the UCK/KLA, in August of 1998. Now, what I'd like to ask first of all is when exactly did you begin helping the UCK/KLA by treating their soldiers. In relation to the time you started the medical team in Turiqevc, was it before, after?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: It was the same -- approximately at the same time. Like, maybe a month before.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough. And in fact, how many other medical care personnel worked with you in treating the UCK/KLA?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: In treating UCK/KLA, we treat -- we treat KLA just like all others , all the other civilians -- I mean all civilian people. We didn't make any distinguishings between KLA and civilians. So we treat them -- all our medical team was engaged with treating both civilians and with UCK/KLAs -- I mean KLA. KLA were members of the houses and people that lived in the same area, so we couldn't treat them in a different way than civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. In the course of treating UCK fighters, did you have occasion to note whether wounded UCK fighters wore uniforms or civilian clothes or was it a case where sometimes they'd wear one and sometimes the other.

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Most of the time they wore uniforms. Sometimes same KLA members would wear civilian clothes as well, which was with my case. I most of the time wore civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You most of the time wore civilian clothes. Did you, in fact, carry a weapon at any time while you were a member of UCK/KLA?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Yes. Once became a member of the KLA, I got a weapon, and I believe this was my reason why I became -- why I became a member of KLA to -- in case to protect myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And while carrying that weapon you at all times wore civilian clothes. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Not all the time. Sometimes I -- I had a uniform, so during my working time I would always work -- wear civilian clothes, but sometimes during -- I mean after my work I would wear a uniform as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And am I correct that you also had relatives within the KLA as well?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Relatives, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What about Zeqir Loshi, whom you identify as a KLA fighter in your statement of 25th September 2001?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: That he fighted as a KLA soldier?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: I don't believe this, but he might have been KLA soldier. And he is not my -- he is not my relative. He is my distant cousin.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: But I do know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you recall whether, in fact, he was a KLA soldier or not?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: I saw him without uniform. I saw him with a gun. He might have been KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, what was the official designation or name of the KLA detachment that you joined in August of 1998?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: There was just a small group of KLA. They were just a group, nothing else. It had no name.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No name. Okay. You mentioned previously the 112 --

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- Brigade --

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So this was a separate group from that?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: This is -- in fact, I just said that the KLA was growing as Serbian forces were -- were -- were being more offensive and perpetrating massacres around and stuff like that, then KLA started to grow.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: And that's what -- I believe these brigades that were formed, they were just some kind of brigades. I wouldn't call them myself brigades because we didn't have too many numbers of soldiers to make brigades and stuff like that. But before that I know that some international analysts and some people from international community would call KLA as -- as terrorist groups. So they figured out that they should organise themselves into what would be close to -- to regular army. And that's how it started to be -- I mean to organise themselves into brigades, to have uniforms, to have their signs, to have a command. But this was just -- I believe this was just an imitation of a regular army, but I wouldn't call this as a regular army myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, am I correct that your detachment fell under the auspices of the so-called Drenica operative zone of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: How many other KLA detachments were you aware of that operated in the Srbica municipality?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you mentioned a whole list of various villages in the area where the UCK/KLA was operating. Are those all in the Srbica municipality?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, did you continue reporting for the TV station during the commencement of the NATO bombings?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: No. Because I didn't have access to a phone because all the phone lines were corrupted.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: And you couldn't -- couldn't do any information.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Prior to that time, during the time-period that you were working for the TV station, am I correct that your KLA colleagues used your role as a journalist with the TV station as a means to have people hear what they wanted about the situation in Srbica; that is to say, did you serve as an information source for the KLA to reach the outside world?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: No. I was serving -- I was -- in fact, I was volunteering as -- I never got paid from TV station so I would be called as a worker of them. I just was volunteering doing my time there. I found that very important since during my life as a student in Pristina I had worked for a newspaper called Bota e Re, which means a new world, and I was a journalist there so I had some experience. And once the war started and I got myself there, I thought -- I found that a good idea if I was engaging myself into information, so people around and there all -- and I mean anyone that could have access to my information would -- would be aware of what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, during the period of 1998 and the early part of 1999, isn't it correct that the KLA in the Drenica operative zone and within the Srbica municipality established roadblocks and attacked Serbian forces?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: I am not aware of these blocks that you are referring to because I was living in Leqin. I myself moved from Runik where I was working as a doctor, and so it was impossible to be there anymore because of Serbian forces that had occupied that area. And just when I moved into Leqin, I didn't have access to those places that you are referring to. But as far as I know myself, KLA soldiers weren't there to attack Serbian forces; they were there to protect themselves and innocent civilian people as much as they could. And that's what their job was. That's what they were trying to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, sir, isn't it a fact that the KLA attacked Serb civilians and Albanian civilians as well as Roma civilians who did not support their armed activities is?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, sir, you talked about being in Leocina and the fact that the Serb civilians had left Leocina. Isn't it a fact that several Serb civilians from the Smigic -- or Zmigic households in Leocina were abducted and killed by the KLA immediately prior to the Serbs leaving the village?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: I don't know about this event.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know whether in fact the -- I just have to wait for the transcript to catch up with us. Do you know if, in fact, the KLA collected a war tax from the civilian population to finance and support its activities?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: No. What I know is that people -- civilian people were helping KLA because KLA members were members of their family as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if I could ask you a couple of questions generally about March 1999 before we move to Izbica specifically. In paragraph 9 of the English statement, the 23rd/25th September 2001 statement that the Prosecution counsel had asked you about, you describe the KLA as not being strong enough to resist the Serbs and that most of the time the KLA was fleeing with the civilians. Now, the question I want to ask you is: When the KLA would flee with the civilians would they take their weapons with them?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: What I said here was that KLA were fleeing because they were not strong enough to protect civilians and to protect themselves from Serbian forces, because Serbian forces had strong machine-guns and arms, so they could never resist them. Most of the time they didn't flee with -- with the civilians. So if there were any of KLA found among civilians, they were with no guns.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What about uniforms, would the KLA when they fled with civilians, would they keep their uniforms or would they change into civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: I must say -- I must say that some of KLA soldiers -- some of KLA soldiers would have fled with civilians in order to take their families in some safer places.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: And when they went there, most of them left. Some of them was very scared of Serbian forces. They might have still be there, but with no arms and with no --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Weapons.

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: -- I mean weapons and no uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let me ask you another question. You indicated that many civilians assisted the KLA and that the KLA had many family members among the civilians. Isn't it a fact that the KLA forces in the area around Izbica specifically ordered the civilian populations from such areas, such as Ozrim and Leocina, to leave those areas and gather in Izbica in and around the 25th and 26th of March, 1999?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: No. No, that never happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now --

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: There was another reason to leave -- I mean for them to leave their houses. There was shelling all over their houses and villages, so they had no choice but to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right. Sir, please, if you could restrict yourself to the questions that I ask --

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: I'm trying.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- because I indicated we have very little time, and I'm trying to ensure that we complete your testimony within the time-period that we have. Now, in your statement you describe how on the 27th of March you went to Tushille and that there were KLA soldiers there among the civilians and that these -- many of these soldiers were with their families. First of all, from what villages were these civilians and KLA from; that is to say, the civilians who were family members of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: From different villages, from very different villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. Now, before we turn to the end of March 1999, in your statement you describe an event on the 20th of March, 1999, when you say you heard about Serb forces surrounding Srbica. Now, first of all, sir, you were not an eye-witness to these events on the 20th of March, 1999, in Srbica, were you?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And did you -- I apologise. Again, I have to slow down. Since we're both speaking English, we have to slow down for the translators. And did you hear from people or did you know through your affiliation with the KLA that the KLA, in fact, had mounted a major assault on the police station in Srbica that morning, the morning of March 20th, 1999, resulting in casualties among the Serbian police forces in Srbica?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: No, I never heard of this, and I believe this never happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. But you were never present to confirm that it didn't happen. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: I wasn't present, but I was told by people who came to -- to see me in my office where I was working as a doctor, and even I treated them and they told me about everything what happened there. So if you want me to describe what I -- what I was -- I mean what I heard from them, I can, but since you want me to --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We have that in your statement, sir.

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There is a suggestion of Serb casualties on that day, including a number killed. Is there some explanation that you can give us for that, or do you just not accept that there were any casualties at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no idea. I don't believe this because I was very close to civilians. I was very close to KLA soldiers, and I never happened to hear such a thing happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, you talked about how the KLA was actually, as you described it, not quite organised but that the idea of it being an army was somewhat of a -- I can't remember if you used the word "illusion" or not. But was it common for groups of KLA fighters to operate independently of one another in a given region such that they would not know what other KLA factions were doing?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: I can't answer this because I don't -- I don't even quite understand your question. I have an idea, but I don't think this -- this is the answer I could help.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you this, sir: In your detachment or group of the KLA, did you know each and every single day what other KLA units in the area, in the neighbouring villages, in the neighbouring hill-sides, what they were doing?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: In -- yeah. I know -- I know that most of them -- I mean, as far as I could get -- got any information at the time, what were they doing in these areas. Maybe not for every one --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, for instance, sir, when you were asked by the Prosecutor about the presence of the KLA in Izbica, I believe that you testified that there -- they may be there, but you're not sure. Would that, in fact, show that your group did not know the whereabouts and the activities of all other KLA forces in the area?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Yeah. When we talk about this, we don't have to do with any kind of activities. We have to do with KLA members who wanted to escape and find refuge in the mountains. So they were all over mountains anywhere they could go. And I know that at that time when Serbian forces started to shell the area, they were told by their commanders that they could go anywhere just to save their lives. So we really don't know where they were. They were hiding themselves. They were into mountains somewhere, and the good thing about that was that Serbian forces never went into mountains to get KLA, but they went in open places and killed the innocent people.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: They didn't chase much KLA --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, now, you were not present to see any persons being killed, were you?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Any persons being killed?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes. In Izbica.

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: You mean I didn't see the process of execution or what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You did not see anyone being killed, in the process of being killed. You were not an eye-witness to any killings?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: No, I wasn't --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: But I saw lots of people that were killed after they were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine, sir. Now, if we focus on Izbica and your knowledge of events there. First of all, you mention one of your friends, this UCK commander Shaban Dragaj. Did you hear from Shaban or from any other persons that you went to Izbica with or spoke with that in fact they had seen local Serbs who had previously resided in Leocina, specifically members of the Zmigic household, that were seen in uniform leading the forces in Izbica, the Serb forces in Izbica?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, are you familiar with a gentleman by the name of Abedin Dragaj also from Leocina who was with Shaban Dragaj when the Serbs entered Izbica?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: I don't know this person.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: I don't believe he was. Because I was with Shaban Dragaj myself lots of times, and I can't remember this Abedin Dragaj. I don't know who he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough. Are you familiar with a KLA soldier by the name of Ramadan Dragaj from Leocina village?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: No, I don't. I don't know this person.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Would you be surprised to find out that you identified Ramadan Dragaj in your September 25th, 2001, statement as one of the three persons who appeared on the film with you, and it says: "Ramadan Dragaj, a KLA soldier from Leqin."

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Ramadan Dragaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In addition to yourself, Zenil [phoen] Loshi and Zabat [phoen] Dragaj, also from Leqin.

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, yes, yes, yes. Yeah. I just forgot his name. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No problem. That's why I'm here to --

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: I know him, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's why I'm here to refresh your recollection. Now let me ask you about this: Do you know whether this Ramadan Dragaj, this KLA soldier, was he related to Shaban Dragaj, Demush Dragaj, or --

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- Mustafa Dragaj?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: They all are cousins, but they would be distant cousins, I guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough. Just waiting for the transcript again. Now, did you hear from your friend Shaban, the KLA commander, or anyone else that you went to Izbica with since you stated that you went there with some friends and some people, did you hear from any of these people that on the fateful day of March the 26th or 27th, 1999, while the civilians were gathered in the lower part of Izbica village that in fact the KLA forces had massed and gathered in the upper part of Izbica village, from where it was planned to attack and resist the Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: No. This never happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Is it correct that -- is it correct that -- well, strike that. Who were the other friends that you went to Izbica village with on the evening of the 30th of March?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: This was Shaban Dragaj, one, the one that I mentioned; the other one -- I mean this was the guy who I went to because I met him in Kopiliq where I was staying myself for the time being, for the day, and we went there together. I believe just him and me. I don't think there was any other person with -- with us. But when we went to Leqin, we met Demush Dragaj, my friend, who I lived in this house before, and we asked for the leader of the village, who was Naim Rexhepi, and these people are the ones that I remember of.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, can you be more specific about that question. You're suggesting here that there's some conflict, possibly a conflict, on 26th or 27th of March envisaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you talk about a plan to attack and resist the Serb forces. What were the Serb forces and where were they?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm responding to the fact that this witness testified that there were two KLA soldiers that were killed on the 27th of March, and he claims that there were no clashes. So I'm wondering how KLA soldiers --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no, but this is a very specific question about a massing of people in one part of the village to attack --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct. We had testimony of this from other witnesses --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- and resist the Serb forces. Now, who are these Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I don't know. It wasn't specified in the evidence that we heard through, I believe, it was Mustafa Dragaj when I confronted him with some of the statements made by Abedin Dragaj in his sworn statement to the OTP regarding what he observed with Shaban Dragaj, the KLA commander, whom Mustafa Dragaj claimed was not a KLA commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can I just make a point here, please? I know myself that Shaban Dragaj during 27th of March and further wasn't he, himself, in Izbica.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct, he was not, he was in the mountains surrounding Izbica.

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: No, he was a little bit farther away. He was in Kopilic mountains, which is not in Izbica, it is even a bit farther. There is another village in between these two parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right. We'll see about that. Now, with respect to your statement of 23 and 25 September 2001, in that statement, in describing on page 4, the second-to-last paragraph on that page you say: "The same evening I went into the village of Izbica together with some friends. One of my friends was Shaban Dragaj, a KLA commander. It was dark when we arrived there, so we could not see the bodies from the massacre, but we heard from people what had happened." Now, I find it odd that this statement from 2001, which you confirmed to be accurate at the time that you testified in the Milosevic proceedings, states that you could not see the bodies; and now today, for the first time, you are telling us that in fact that evening you could and in fact did see the bodies at the location where they were killed.

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but what you're saying here -- okay, is this your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I haven't gotten to my question yet.

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The question I want to ask you is, sir: When you read the statement dated the 23rd and 25th of September, 2001, in the English language before signing it, did you in fact read this portion of it and confirm that this was true to the investigator from the OTP?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: First of all, I want to answer in the comment you made just before this because I feel responsible of that. I want you to clarify that even in the Milosevic case I made it clear that I saw the bodies. You have to take the statement once again and read -- go through it and see that I made it clear that there was a mistake in the statement, so I wanted to correct it and I did. And if I didn't pay attention -- I mean attention to every word when I signed the statement, I don't see this of a big deal.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, am I correct that Shaban Dragaj was with you when you decided to obtain a camera and film the site in Izbica?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And in fact, would it be accurate to state that -- now, I know you -- once the -- once Mr. Thaqi arrived with the camera, then several -- you were not with Mr. Thaqi and the camera the entire time, but during that portion of the time when the bodies were being filmed and when the burial was being prepared, is it correct that Shaban Dragaj was still with you and in fact was involved in organising and leading the efforts to film the bodies and to prepare for the burial of the bodies?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: No, no. I believe he even wasn't there. I mean, this day maybe he was and maybe he was [sic]. I can't remember. I was so busy myself, but I never recall that he was there. He still might have been. I'm not being much specific about this. But he didn't take place -- he didn't take place with taping and stuff like that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, this Sefedin Thaqi, who actually had the camera and did the filming, do you know whether he was in fact a KLA member?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: He wasn't. Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Good. Now, I'd like to ask you about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just before you move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In your -- in the transcript of the Milosevic trial you were asked the question: "Was Shaban Dragaj present with you all the time?" This is when you're filming.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was with me all the time when I went in the evening by May the 30th, he was with me all the time, that's correct, but not the next day because I had my own things to do. I was busy, like I said, with my own things as -- my own business as a doctor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you also in fact go on to say: "We were not able to see the bodies clearly" --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: "But the truth is we did see them and that is what I stated." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, I have a question to clear up with your statement of 19 May 1999. The first page of that statement you're describing the videotape that we've seen portions of here today. And you say in that statement under oath: "I recorded this videotape myself on March 31st, 1999, and this original exhibit has been in my constructive possession from the time of filming until now." Now, we already know, thanks to the testimony that you gave in your subsequent statements as well as here today, that in fact this statement you made under oath is not true and accurate because Mr. Thaqi is the one who recorded the video. Now, is it also the case that the second part of this statement, that is to say that you had the original tape in your constructive possession at all times before delivery to the Prosecutor, that statement is not accurate and in fact is false. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: No. This is correct, but I believe this is a misunderstanding. Because what I was -- what I said there or what I was trying to explain there, and I did -- I believe I did so, was that just after the taping was done by Sefedin Thaqi in -- after a few days, I believe this was April 3rd or 4th, I can't remember it now, we transferred the whole filming from his tape to VHS tape, which I had it all the time in my possession. But that tape I couldn't bring with myself to Albania because I found it very dangerous to take it with myself. Later on I meant I could and I would, but I never did because I found it too dangerous. And then I was trying to get a hold of Sefedin Thaqi's tape, which I did. And this is how this Sefedin Thaqi's tape got into Tribunal and not my tape that you're referring to, which, of course, like you said, was in my possession all the time. And I believe now it's in a possession of Tribunal of The Hague as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, with respect to Mr. Thaqi's tape, am I correct that this tape was at one point in time stolen by some thieves?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Yes. At the time where I was looking for this tape, his own camera was stolen, I believe not because of the tape but because -- the tape was stolen because of camera. The thieves didn't even know what was in. And then with the help of Shaban Dragaj I get a hold of this tape again.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You say with the help of Shaban Dragaj. Were the persons who had stolen the camera, were they members of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, as far as the filming of the tape is concerned, you had already stated that you did not accompany at all times Mr. Thaqi as he filmed. Now, in particular with the segment that we saw earlier today, the first segment where we saw the set of bodies, as a medical doctor would you have expected there to be more blood at such a dramatic and large-numbered amount of corpses in the same location, particularly more blood on the ground surrounding these bodies?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Would I expect it as a medical doctor?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: But I'm telling you that I saw lots of blood there. And if you look carefully at those tape, you will be able to see some of it too.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I have -- now -- strike that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you think this tape has been doctored in any way or does it represent what you saw at the scene?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't think so, that -- because I have the other VHS tape which is in Tribunal possession now, and these two can be compared very easily.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, is it correct that you do not even know the exact location where this first group of bodies was filmed?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: No, I know the correct location. What I didn't know when I was asked by Prosecutor, first of all, was that he showed to me a picture with faces that cannot be recognised. I mean, from the picture, you cannot say if you don't see the faces then you cannot tell where they were. But as we went on through the -- through the film -- I mean through the tape, I was able to recognise the places.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we can move on to the actual burials themselves. You've already identified that certain KLA soldiers were among those that had been -- that had been buried there at the location in Izbica, and you mentioned certain other people from other locations. Is it correct that some bodies buried at this location were brought from elsewhere, specifically from villages as far away as the Klina municipality?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but you make me laugh at this because it is correct that some of people were from Klina, but these people were gathered here in order to find refuge. And these people were killed there. These were old people. You have the names there, and you might be able to see how old they were. So there were people from Jashanica, which is -- which belonged to the municipality of Klina, elderly people, and there were people from different parts of Drenica that had come to Izbica because they thought it would be a much safer place than elsewhere. So that's how you find these people from Klina that have been killed in Izbica.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you be surprised to find out that one of the survivors from Izbica came here and testified and said that bodies were brought from other locations in the months following the Izbica burial and buried in the Izbica location? That's what I was referring to, sir.

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: I know that later on there were other -- after this massacre happened there were some bodies -- some other people or soldiers who died and they were brought in the same burial site just because they didn't want to dig graves in other places.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. So we do follow each other. Now, as far as the number of persons buried at Izbica at that time, that is to say the end of March 1999, am I correct that you don't know how many bodies were precisely from the massacre, since bodies were brought from other locations to the grave-site, and you and the others viewed all the bodies as being victims of the conflict with no need to categorise where and from whence they came from? And I'm trying to find out whether that's what you meant in your statement of 23/25 September at page 28, paragraph 6, when you uttered those words. That is to say, of the 127 bodies that were buried there that day, you don't know exactly how many of those were from the massacre that you described hearing about from other people, do you?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I don't have any more questions for this witness. I do believe at least some of my colleagues do. So hopefully we have enough time for them. I tried to be brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Just one matter you could clarify in relation to this last question. You're saying that you don't know exactly how many of these that were buried there that day were from the massacre. So where else might they have been from, the ones that were buried that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, you have there two large groups of people, two large groups, and the other one -- the first large group is made up by two groups again. And then you have other -- other people found around. And I just explained it before that there was people that were found in those other spots, other places, still in Izbica itself. And these people were from -- from there. So they might have gotten killed in different events, they might have gotten killed in the same event. I wasn't there. I don't know. But most of the people who were there were taken from these two large groups, and these were the people that were buried there. And there was two soldiers that I was referring to. So this is my explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, but that explanation relates only to people who were buried there at the time you showed the preparations for the burial on the video.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't understand what you said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That explanation relates only to people who were buried there at the time we saw the burial --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- preparations on the video.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And we've just been hearing that there were later people brought from elsewhere and buried in the same place.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, even after -- like when we taped it, there were 127 people that were buried in the same grave-site. And later on I heard that -- I wasn't there, I was in Albania at that period of time. There was some other people, they might have been KLA soldiers killed afterwards were buried in the same -- in the same place. Or civilians, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I'd like just to ask just one question to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Relating specifically to the persons, the 127 persons who were buried at that grave-site on or about March the 30th or 31st of 1999, in your statement you say on page 28: "Finally, I will say that I am not quite sure how many of the 127 persons we buried at the grave-site actually were from the massacre. Some of these bodies were brought to the grave-site from other locations. They were all victims of the conflict, and we did not at that time categorise the bodies from where they were killed." Now, by that, did you mean that there were persons in addition to the two soldiers that you have identified, the KLA soldiers, additional persons that were brought from other locations to Izbica to be buried at the location. Is that what these words in your statement mean?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: No, no. When I say -- when I say they were, like you said, about -- you mentioned the word "conflict." The word "conflict" was used in a sense of being in conflict, Albanians and Serbians, for a long time, and during this war as well, but not for a combat or something. This doesn't have to do with a combat. I have explained this even in my previous testimony with Milosevic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: But with respect to -- but with respect to who where -- here you're talking about the burials that took place of the persons on that day, and even in your own words, if I go down further, you say you would estimate the number of people from the massacre to be between 110 and 120 persons. So based upon my arithmetic, that would mean that at least -- at least 7 if not 17 persons came from other locations.

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So obviously you had knowledge of it in 2001 when this statement was taken.

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Yes. There were some people like -- just when we were talking about the women that was killed in the -- I mean, was buried by Serbian forces -- who was burned by Serbian forces in the tractor and she was taken in the same place as well, and there was some other civilians that were killed in some different places because when Serbian forces entered in --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's all I wanted to find out, sir --

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: -- they killed anyone they got.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, I think I've gotten the clarification that I needed, Your Honour. I'm completed again, for the second time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do have a couple of questions. Thank you, Your Honour, very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Loshi, I'm Djuro Cepic --

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: I don't have translation in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Number 4 is the channel, if you can move the ...

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon or good evening, Mr. Loshi. I'm Djuro Cepic, one of the attorneys on the Defence team of Mr. Lazarevic. Several times today you confirmed that you had seen those bodies that were filmed, and on page 40 of the transcript at the explicit question of my learned friend Ms. Kravetz, you responded that none of the bodies were dressed in a uniform. Do you stand by that statement, Mr. Loshi?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Yes, I stand by my statement that none of the bodies that were taken from massacre site where we filmed were in the uniforms. But if you are talking and referring for the uniforms that were found in -- in the -- the grave-site or burial site, I would clarify that there was a member of KLA and his name was Ajet Beqiri who was killed by 27th of March together with his friend and member of KLA as well, whose name was Zaim Bajrami. But Zaim Bajrami was a KLA member, but he wasn't wearing a uniform; he was in civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And this first one was buried in the uniform of the so-called KLA. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Yeah. Ajet Beqiri was buried in KLA uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And were there any other persons wearing parts of uniform among those who were filmed?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your statement is quite voluminous, the one from 2001. And I will only remind you on page 24, paragraph 1 of the English version you name Ajet Beqiri, born in 1960, and you state that he was killed as a KLA fighter, fighting man. There is something illogical here, but I think that was clarified in the Milosevic trial. In a statement you said it was after the massacre, and later you corrected that to the 27th. On the next page, however, it is stated, that's tape 31.49 and 31.54 seconds, it is stated that the first one had a soldier's green jacket and the other one had a military green coat. Is that your -- that is your statement. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: I don't remember I said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: If you don't remember, it is in your statement. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: I don't believe -- I didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Did you sign the statement in 2001?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Sure I did. I believe you are misinterpreting my statement because, as far as I know, there was only one soldier wearing uniform, if you mean in the day of burying these people from the massacre, and his name was Ajet Beqiri. I don't -- I am not aware that somebody else had any part of uniform or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Loshi, I quoted your statement page 25 of the English version, but if that is your evidence we will move on. Page 4, paragraph 4 of the English version; page 3, last paragraph you describe how you stayed in Tusilje village until 29th March and then we heard the rest of your story about how you continued to move. While you were in Tushille village, did you hear of any fighting going on, namely that KLA was fighting in nearby villages?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: No, there was no fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And do you know where Likovac village is?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Yes, I know, but I wasn't there that time and I had no connection with Likovc. I cannot tell anything about Likovc.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And you never heard that policemen were killed there on the 26th of March and policemen were wounded on the 24th of March. Is that your evidence today?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Yeah. I'd been suggested about this in Milosevic case by Milosevic himself, and I just didn't know about that. I said it might have happened, but it doesn't matter to me because my testimony is related to Izbica. And I even said there and I am saying now that there is no excuse for Serbian forces if there was -- there was any combat involvement of KLA in Likovc that they -- that Serbian --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, we've heard that.

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... innocent people in Izbica.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [In English] Mr. Loshi, I just specified my question.

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Okay, but you don't have to interrupt me either.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Okay, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Loshi.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I haven't got any further questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, just give me a moment to ask one question which may give rise to something. The discussion you've had just a moment ago about the uniforms, what it says on page 25 of your statement is: "Man, grey/black sweater, military green jacket." And then the following description is: "Man, bluish jacket" --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- "military green overcoat, covered in a grey/red woolen blanket." And so far as the identity of each of these is concerned, the entry is unknown. Now, the suggestion that's being made to you is that these may be examples of uniforms being worn by these victims. Can you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Now I got exactly what he meant, and thank you very much for these explanations. Because there is -- in my testimony there is a part of that whole testimony that I didn't do it myself. It's a part of -- of the investigator who -- who did those columns, and it should be in those columns. Is it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. So that wasn't my comment about that. They -- he might have -- might have had some other witnesses describing those or he might have described them himself, but it's not what I said about this. And I believe there is an explanation in this testimony somewhere about this if you read it carefully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's unfortunate that that should be the case because of course you've signed each page --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- of your statement at the end, and you've therefore adopted this as your own evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I signed all of it. But again, Your Honour, I would ask you to go through the statement and once again to see that there is an explanation of -- in -- of investigator, that he made it clear that not all of it that was -- especially in these columns was something that I was giving comments. I did in some of it but not in all of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, the statement says: "The investigator has numbered the photos captured from the video and made a list of the bodies in this group. I have put in the names of the persons mentioned in the tape according to the recording made by Sefedin Thaqi and placed the names on the list as follows." So you say it's the names that you're responsible for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There should be another passage, as far as I remember, there should be somewhere -- I cannot say which passage is that, but there should be another passage which clarifies this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry in taking you through this trouble, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You'll be given a copy of the statement in a moment to see if you can identify that; I hope there is a copy handy for that purpose. But the question is this: Noting that these descriptions were entered by someone who viewed the tape, are these indicative of the bodies wearing uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Is this indicative --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. Do these descriptions indicate that these were persons who were actually wearing uniform when they were killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was one -- only one person which I was referring to as a name -- as -- his name was Ajet Beqiri.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I know that, that's on page 24.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But if you look at page 25 now, you'll be shown it, and halfway down you'll see these two descriptions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You'll see the two names unknown together halfway down the page, if you have page 24 -- 25.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, read the description next to the two names unknown.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. "Man, grey/black sweater, military green jacket." And then who else is with military -- oh, okay, another one. "Man, bluish jacket, military green overcoat, covered in a grey/red woolen blanket."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, does that help you to tell us whether any of the bodies, apart from the two KLA soldiers --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- were actually clad in what might be described as a uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would be happy to help you with this, but I really can't. I mean, there is no reason for me to be reluctant to give this information because I don't find that much important, but I just don't remember that there was another KLA member buried in Izbica event except Ajet Beqiri, that might have been someone else. And all of these descriptions -- I just wanted to make it clear, and it should be somewhere said here, because I read it myself, were made by investigator. And of course I was asked to sign it and I just signed it. I don't think this would be so much contradictive or whatever so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes, very briefly, Your Honours. I just have a couple questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mr. Loshi, during cross-examination you were asked about the number of the victims buried at the grave-site that we saw in the video, and you were read a paragraph on page 28 of your statement and -- which indicates that there were 127 persons buried; and you say there that you would estimate the number from the massacres to be from 110 and 120. The remainder of the persons, were those persons who had -- based on information you were able to gather, were those persons who had been killed on that same day as those persons killed in the massacre?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: I wasn't there for -- from -- I mean in the -- in Izbica, I wasn't there from the 27th of March, so I don't even know what happened and who -- and who was killed where -- who where was killed. But based on my best knowledge, I will say here that these people were killed either by 28th or, like we say -- we have two soldiers killed by 27th, and even for these two soldiers I know from other people what they have said to me. So I'm -- I am not -- I am not aware exactly what they -- what they -- all of them were killed except these 28 of -- I mean 28th March that were killed, these two large -- large groups of people. But I believe all of them were killed in -- by 27th and 28th because I know that by 26th of March there was no killed anybody. I was there myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And based on what you were told, other than these two persons you referred to as KLA soldiers, were the remainder of the persons civilians?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Yes, except these two people that I was referring to, Ajet Beqiri and Zaim -- what was his last name? Zaim Bajrami.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now moving on to a different subject. You were asked about your involvement with the KLA, and you indicated that you treated KLA soldiers. Did you have any other type of involvement with the KLA, either in 1998 or 1999?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Not really.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Did you ever participate in any type of combat operation --

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Oh, no, no, never.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And were you -- I'm sorry. Did you have any access to information about combat operations that were being organised or any other type of logistic operation that was being organised by the KLA, by other KLA members?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: From --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: In your capacity as a doctor.

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: I was informed for most of actions if they happened, if there was any. But as I have said there, there was -- KLA was really weak comparing to Serbian army forces and there were not much fighting between KLA and -- and Serbian forces at this period of time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Loshi, that completes your evidence. Thank you for coming again to the Tribunal to give evidence, and you're now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, having me here to testify in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, thank you for assisting us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, what's to happen now?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I have the unenviable task to announce, Your Honour, that we have run out of witnesses for this week. We had scheduled K -- a witness without a pseudonym; I do not want to call his name. We have received a report that a subpoena was not served; I think that was filed today or yesterday. He was a witness that was scheduled for four hours in chief and that would have taken up -- and that would have enabled us to fill the week with witnesses. We have spoken with him and he did indicate hesitancy in coming and made statements relating to security. So although his name was mentioned previously, I do not want to mention it now in case there are issues in respect to security. So that is the reason why we are not in a position to -- to put forward a witness for the remainder of the week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the Chamber's of the view that every day has to be used to best advantage in view of the time it will inevitably take for this trial to be completed. You know that already, not only because of what we've said but because of what we did in respect of failure to have witnesses present to occupy the time. It will be obvious to you, therefore, that we have in mind to allocate some of the lost time, at least, to your overall allocation of time. And I'll hear you on any comments you want to make about that before we take a decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would just ask that you consider that the -- where witnesses who are expected to fill a substantial amount of time fail to turn up, for whatever reason - and we are not sure about the reason, and we have done everything, including obtaining subpoenas to get the witness here - it is, to some degree, beyond our control, but I know it is indicated that we should have a witness in reserve. But if this witness had attended then the shorter witnesses who have testified would be witnesses in reserve. So there are occasions when things are really outside of the hands -- outside of the control of the parties, inescapable occurrences, which I'd ask you to bear in mind when you consider making an order in respect to the time available to the Prosecution. That is the only comment I have on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We do not for one moment accept that these are factors beyond the control of the Prosecution which have caused this situation. It's clear that there was always a question mark over the willingness of the witness referred to to be here. That's plainly a situation where there should be ample other witnesses available to cover, so this was a particularly bad example of a failure by the Prosecution to take reasonable steps to ensure that time is used properly. Therefore, we are all agreed that some part of the time lost must be allocated against the Prosecution's overall allocation. We differ on the extent, and by a majority we'll allocate one-half of tomorrow --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- one-half of tomorrow's lost time to the Prosecution's allocation. I say "by a majority"; the dissenting member of the Bench would have allocated a larger amount -- proportion of the time than that. We altogether, however, consider the decision made to be an extremely generous to the Prosecution, in view of the history of matters so far and what's been said so far; and we hope that that will be a clear warning that this situation should not be repeated. We'll now adjourn and resume at 9.00 on Monday.
